glossary.et: Evapotranspiration is the water that evaporates from the soil plus the water plants release. ET₀ estimates that loss for a standard reference crop surface.
glossary.ndvi: NDVI uses reflected light to show how much green vegetation a satellite detects.
glossary.soilMoisture: This is the water in the soil. In the root zone, it indicates how much water plants can access.
glossary.waterBalance: This compares water coming in through rain and irrigation with water leaving through evapotranspiration, runoff, and drainage.
glossary.frost: This is the chance that cold will damage a crop. It depends on temperature, how long the cold lasts, and the crop’s growth stage.
glossary.satellite: A satellite estimates conditions across a wide area. A ground measurement describes one spot in a parcel. Together they help explain local differences.

frost.title: Hard frost
frost.what: A −3 °C night burns leaves and flowers of sensitive crops.
frost.action: Irrigate the evening before, cover nurseries and avoid potato or bean in frost weeks.

heat.title: Heat wave
heat.what: Highs of 34 °C: sensitive crops close their pores and water demand rises 15%.
heat.action: Irrigate early or at night and give priority to flowering crops.

drought.title: Drought / water cut
drought.what: The water users' board cuts allocations due to low water in the upper basin.
drought.action: Leave plots fallow or with legumes and switch high-value crops to drip.

heavyRain.title: Heavy rain
heavyRain.what: Too much humidity: fungi on sensitive crops and soil washing off bare plots.
heavyRain.action: Improve drainage, apply preventive fungicide and cover bare soil.

pests.title: Pest outbreak
pests.what: A pest spreads; it hits harder where many plots share the same family.
pests.action: Scout weekly, control early and mix families in your rotation.

dry.title: Reservoir empty
dry.what: Your water for the year ran out: crops dry out and yield less.
dry.action: Plant less area, switch to rotations with legumes or improve irrigation.

climate.title: Real frost or heat
climate.what: According to NASA POWER, this month had days outside what some of your crops tolerate.
climate.action: Check those crops' planting dates or choose more tolerant varieties.

waterPeak.title: High-demand month
waterPeak.what: Most plots need more water than your monthly share.
waterPeak.action: Plan irrigation turns or store water in the reservoir in earlier months.

monoculture.title: Monoculture pest risk
monoculture.what: Over half the farm is one family: pests and diseases spread easily.
monoculture.action: Mix different families on neighboring plots and rotate every season.

erosion.title: Erosion on bare plots
erosion.what: With heavy rain, uncovered soil washes away and loses organic matter.
erosion.action: Plant a cover crop or leave stubble on those plots.

et.title: Water the field loses (ET)
et.short: Sun, heat and wind pull water out of the soil and the leaves.
et.text: It's the water that leaves the field into the air: what evaporates from the soil and what the plant "sweats" through its leaves. More sun, heat, wind and dry air mean more water lost.
et.how: We compute reference ET (ET0) for every day of the last 21 years with the FAO Penman-Monteith equation.
et.source: NASA POWER (temperature, radiation, humidity and wind)

kc.title: How thirsty each crop is (Kc)
kc.short: Each crop drinks more or less water depending on its age.
kc.text: Each crop uses a different share of ET0 depending on its size. Just planted it needs little (low Kc); at full bloom it needs more than the reference grass (Kc above 1).
kc.how: Your crop's water is Kc × ET0, day by day, following its stages: initial, development, mid and late.

balance.title: How much to irrigate
balance.short: What the crop needs, minus rain, plus what the irrigation system loses.
balance.text: What the crop needs minus the rain it can use is your net irrigation. No system is perfect: furrow irrigation loses almost half the water, drip very little. That total is gross irrigation.
balance.how: We compare each rotation's gross irrigation with your available water. If it isn't enough, we show how many m³/ha you are short and in how many of the 21 years it would have been enough. 1 mm of water = 10 m³ per hectare.

ndvi.title: Plant greenness (NDVI)
ndvi.short: Satellites see how green and healthy the plants are.
ndvi.text: A number satellites compute from the light plants reflect. A healthy green plant reflects a lot of infrared: high NDVI. Bare or dry soil: low NDVI.
ndvi.how: You see it on the map and in the Time machine, month by month since 2000.
ndvi.source: NASA MODIS Terra, via NASA GIBS

soil.title: Soil moisture
soil.short: How much water is left in the soil where the roots are.
soil.text: How much water the soil holds where the roots are. In the Majes desert, without irrigation, the soil is dry almost all year; in the highlands it rises in the rainy season.
soil.how: We show natural soil moisture by month and week, plus the SMAP root-zone moisture map.
soil.source: NASA POWER (GWETROOT) and NASA SMAP L4

frost.title: Frost and heat
frost.short: How often each week of the year got too cold or too hot.
frost.text: Frost burns leaves and flowers when the air drops below a certain temperature; extreme heat closes the plant's pores and lowers yield. Each crop has its own limit.
frost.how: We count in how many of the last 21 years each week had frost (minimum of 2 °C or less) or heat.
frost.source: NASA POWER (daily minimum and maximum temperature)

fusion.title: Altitude adjustment
fusion.short: We correct satellite climate data for your field's real altitude.
fusion.text: Satellite climate data comes in squares of about 50 km with an average altitude. Majes is at 1,400 m, but its neighboring squares are at 835 m (coast) and 1,941 m.
fusion.how: We measure your field's real altitude with NASA terrain data and blend the two climate squares around it.

ground.title: Satellite vs. ground station
ground.short: A station measures one spot well; satellites cover everything.
ground.text: A station measures one point very well. Satellites cover the whole planet every day, with less detail. Together they complement each other: the station checks and corrects the satellite.
ground.how: We prepared the comparison with the SENAMHI Pampa de Majes station to measure the satellite error.

range.title: Ranges, not one number
range.short: Every year is different, so we show the typical value and the extremes.
range.text: Weather changes every year: dry years, normal years and El Niño. So we don't give one number but a range: the typical value and what happens in good and bad years.
range.how: Every figure comes from simulating the 21 real years: we show the median and the 10%–90% range.

rotation.title: Crop rotation
rotation.short: Changing crops each season breaks pests and feeds the soil.
rotation.text: Alternating crops from different families breaks pest cycles. Legumes (faba, beans, alfalfa) fix nitrogen from the air and feed the soil. Leaving the field bare makes erosion easier.
rotation.how: The "soil health" score rewards legumes, family variety and covered soil, and penalizes bare months.
rotation.source: General agronomic rules (to validate with an agronomist)

point.legumeN: Legumes in the group ({crops}): they fix nitrogen from the air, about {kg} kg/ha, free fertilizer for the soil.
point.noLegume: No legume in the group: all nitrogen must come from fertilizer.
point.nDeficit: The group needs a lot of nitrogen (about {kg} kg/ha short): high fertilizer cost.
point.nBalanced: Nitrogen is balanced between what they need and what they fix.
point.laborPeak: {crops} need a lot of labor: check you have enough hands.
point.roots: Roots at different depths: they use water and nutrients from different layers.
point.sameFamily: Two crops of the same family in a row: pests and diseases carry over.
point.breaksPests: Three different families: breaks pest and disease cycles.
point.twoFamilies: Alternates two families: helps somewhat against pests.
point.legumeBeforeHungry: {a} leaves nitrogen in the soil for {b}, which is very demanding.
point.hungryAfterHungry: {b} comes right after {a}: two very demanding crops in a row deplete the soil.
point.potatoRepeat: Several nightshades (potato, tomato, paprika) in the same cycle: more late blight and pests. Space them out.
point.overlap: Two crops overlap for {days} days: check the planting months.
point.bareMonths: The soil stays bare for {n} months: more erosion and organic matter loss.
point.alwaysCovered: The soil is covered all year.
point.sharedPestsRotation: They share {n} pest(s) or disease(s): watch for carry-over between seasons.
point.sameFamilyTogether: Two crops of the same family together: they share pests and compete the same way.
point.nCompetition: {crops} compete for nitrogen: you'll need more fertilizer.
point.heights: Different heights: they use light better without shading each other.
point.waterCompetition: {crops} need a lot of water at the same time.
point.weedSensitive: {crops} can't compete with weeds: frequent weeding and no dense plants nearby.
point.noSharedSeason: Their seasons barely overlap: they don't really grow together. Adjust the planting month.
point.sharedPestsTogether: They share {n} pest(s) or disease(s): one outbreak hits both at once.

companion.milpa: {a} and {b} are the classic milpa: beans fix nitrogen and climb the maize.
companion.legumeTall: {a} and {b}: the legume provides nitrogen and they grow to different heights.
companion.andeanPair: {a} and {b} are a traditional Andean pairing: the legume provides nitrogen.
companion.alliumLegume: {a} and {b} don't mix: garlic and onion hold back the growth of legumes.
companion.shadeHungry: {a} and {b}: one shades the other and both need a lot of nitrogen.
companion.perennialDense: Alfalfa is perennial and very dense: it competes hard. Better use it in rotation.
companion.threeSisters: {a} and {b} are part of the "three sisters": the squash covers the ground and keeps moisture in.
companion.cerealLegume: {a} and {b} are a classic cereal and legume mix: more forage, and richer.
companion.carrotOnion: {a} and {b} grow well together: different roots, and the smell keeps carrot pests away.
companion.alliumRepels: {a} and {b} get along: garlic and onion help keep some pests away.
companion.nightshadeBlight: {a} and {b} share late blight: an outbreak on one quickly reaches the other.

care.cuts: Cut every 35 to 40 days; let it regrow before the next cut.
care.aphids: Watch for aphids, especially in dry and hot periods.
care.noTrampling: Don't graze or walk on it when the soil is wet.
care.hilling: Hill up at 30 to 45 days to protect the tubers.
care.lateBlight: Late blight (Phytophthora): appears with humidity or rain; prevent with fungicide and good drainage.
care.andeanWeevil: Andean weevil: rotate and clear residues from the previous season.
care.rotation3y: Don't plant potato on the same plot again for 3 years.
care.transplant: Sown in a nursery and transplanted after 6 to 8 weeks.
care.weeding: Frequent weeding: shallow roots, it can't compete with weeds.
care.thrips: Thrips: more damaging with heat and drought; check the leaves.
care.stopIrrigation: Stop irrigating 2 to 3 weeks before harvest for proper curing.
care.splitN: Split nitrogen into 2 or 3 doses (planting, development and before flowering).
care.armyworm: Fall armyworm: check the whorl in the first weeks.
care.floweringWater: Don't let it lack water at flowering: that's when irrigation pays off most.
care.chocolateSpot: Chocolate spot: appears with humidity; avoid evening irrigation.
care.coldTolerant: Tolerates cold better than other crops (down to about −3 °C).
care.frostSensitive: Very frost-sensitive: don't plant if there is frost risk in the cycle.
care.rust: Rust: orange spots on leaves; use tolerant varieties.
care.whitefly: Whitefly: more common in heat; control early.
care.birds: Protect the seed heads from birds near harvest.
care.downyMildewQuinoa: Downy mildew: appears with humidity; don't overwater.
care.saponin: Wash the grain to remove saponin (bitter taste) before selling or eating it.
care.coldStart: Plant it in the cool months: it needs cold to form good bulbs.
care.looseSoil: Needs loose, stone-free soil so the roots grow straight.
care.thinning: Thin the seedlings 3 to 4 weeks after sowing.
care.evenWater: Water evenly: irregular irrigation cracks fruits and roots.
care.trellis: Give it stakes or a trellis to climb.
care.coolSeason: Prefers cool weather: avoid the hottest months.
care.powderyMildew: Powdery mildew: white powder on the leaves, more common in dry, warm weather.
care.dryHarvest: Harvest when the grain is dry and hard.
care.droughtTolerant: Handles dry spells better than other cereals.
care.cutAtMilk: Cut it for forage when the grain is still milky.
care.withVetch: Mixed with pea or vetch it gives richer forage.
care.groundCover: Its big leaves cover the soil and keep moisture in.
care.pollinators: Needs bees to pollinate the flowers.
care.staking: Stake and prune it so the fruit stays off the ground.
care.sunDrying: Dry the pods in the sun on clean ground after harvest.

group.nCover: Legumes cover {pct} of the nitrogen these crops need.
group.nNone: No legumes: all the nitrogen has to come from fertilizer.
